newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian MFK, Renaissance say in world-class merger.
newsitem.headline: Russian MFK, Renaissance say in world-class merger.

text.p: Russia's financial landscape changed on Wednesday with the merger of Bank MFK and Renaissance Capital into what they said is the largest domestic investment bank.

MFK-Renaissance, which has hopes of international stature but plans to concentrate on the Russian market, will have $400 million equity capital, total assets of $2 billion and a further $1 billion under management, the companies said.
"This has the possibility of becoming a bank of world stature," Boris Jordan, CEO of the new company, told a news conference.
Officials said the new bank would work independently from the powerful Unexim-MFK financial industrial group which owns half the new firm and will provide a large chunk of its work.
"The Renaissance group has positive control over the company," said Jordan, previously head of Renaissance Capital. MFK, also known as ICFI, and Renaissance shareholders each own 50 percent of it.
"The company is outside of the Unexim group," Jordan said. "That was an absolutely mandatory part of the deal."

Renaissance Capital and Bank MFK are both active in trading and issuing Russian securities and corporate finance. The central bank said recently that Uneximbank was Russia's third largest bank by assets and Bank MFK was fifteenth.

The new firm will feel the strong hand of former first deputy prime minister Vladimir Potanin, the young businessman who controls Uneximbank and its assets, like control over a big slice of Norilsk Nickel, a global mining and refining giant.
Potanin will be chairman of the new firm.

"Potanin is simply consolidating the expertise he had in the group into two institutions, a commercial bank and investment bank," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) Moscow managing director Nick Jordan. Uneximbank is a commercial bank.
MFK was a minority shareholder in Renaissance, but Renaissance says MFK has only 50 percent of the new firm and does not have an indirect majority through Renaissance Capital holdings.
DMG's Jordan said the merger between two related domestic banks would not have a strong effect in Russia, where domestic banks have begun to work as allies with foreign banks.
"We see them (Russian banks) as partner not competitor," he said. "Five or ten years down the line it might be different, but I don't think they have the capital in the short term."

Uneximbank has ambitious plans to acquire the Norilsk stake owned by the government which it manages, and it may put up $500 million of its own funds if it decides to make a bid for Svyazinvest telecom holding company.
But it is discussing financing with Deutsche Bank and other banks to gather the $1.18 billion minimum price tag of the 25 percent stake up for auction this month.
Svyazinvest owns controlling stakes in 88 regional and other operators and Potanin said his group, so far without a telecom operator, would take a strong management hand if it bid and won.
"If we win, we will take part in management," Potanin said after the news conference announcing the merger.
